metadata.title: Final Trump arch plans submitted to city omit proposed military complex

sources.news_title: Trump Appears to Have Dropped the ‘Military Complex’ Justification for His Arch
sources.text:
President Donald Trump turned course last month when he said his proposed 250-foot arch would have a military complex attached. But new documents indicate that Trump’s security plans — which seemed to be a late addition meant to boost the project’s chances — are not part of the final plan.
Trump’s push to highlight the project’s military importance came as the arch drew deep scrutiny for its hefty multimillion-dollar price tag. However, plans published by the National Capital Planning Commission made no mention of defense facilities.
On Sept. 20, Trump said the military requested that the Memorial Circle project house a “top-grade military complex.” That proposal would have housed, stored and allowed use of large numbers of drones and snipers on both the roof and plaza areas, in addition to storing large quantities of sniper ammunition.
The final project plans, as published by the Interior Department, include construction of the Triumphal Arch’s associated plaza and landscape improvements, supporting utility and stormwater infrastructure, traffic and pedestrian circulation modifications, security features, lighting and temporary staging and laydown areas.
Trending
There are no indications the project will include military infrastructure based on the submitted details.
Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.
In an emailed statement to The Washington Sun, the Interior Department said the arch’s current design is capable of accommodating the national security function mentioned in the president’s Truth Social post. The Pentagon referred The Washington Sun to the White House, which did not respond to a request for comment.
The DOI maintains the arch will enhance the visitor experience at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
The proposed concrete structure has drawn criticism from flight attendants and veterans, who warn it could pose safety risks to pilots and obstruct landmark views. The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA denounced Trump’s plans, arguing the project would pose a threat to aviation safety.
The flight attendants’ union said the arch would interfere with planes’ final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and cited safety concerns stemming from the Jan. 29, 2025, crash in which an American Airlines commercial plane and an Army helicopter collided midair over the Potomac River, killing 67 people.
“DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path,” said the association’s president, Sara Nelson. “Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles, or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always.”
In a statement issued in September, the Federal Aviation Administration said the arch would not pose a safety hazard to aircraft.
Experts reviewed airspace, air traffic patterns and procedures around the airport, as well as operations at nearby military/public-use airports and found the arch would be appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed toward the arch to make it noticeable to pilots, the FAA said.
Despite promoting the project as a memorial to military service, three veterans have sued the Trump administration to bar it from erecting the arch without congressional approval, stating the “view of the Lincoln Memorial from Arlington House will be obscured, disrupting the historic and symbolic link between the two.”
The National Capital Planning Commission has scheduled a hearing on Nov. 5 to discuss the prospective arch.

sources.news_title: Plans for ‘Arc de Trump’ military complex abandoned
sources.text:
The final plans for Donald Trump’s 250ft-tall triumphal arch do not include the “top-grade military complex” the US president said he would add.
In September, Mr Trump said the “Arc de Trump”, as the proposed monument has been nicknamed, would be used to store and launch drones, as well as provide a sniper perch.
A tranche of new documents was released by the National Capital Planning Commission on Friday. None of the documents mentioned a military purpose for the arch.
“At the strong request of the United States military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch... into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch,” Mr Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform in September.
“There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world. Out of the 59 top cities and capitals, Washington, DC, IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH, but it will now and, by far, the greatest of them all!”

sources.news_title: Trump’s final arch blueprints quietly torpedo his ‘top grade’ sales pitch: report
sources.text:
FILE PHOTO: Vehicles drive past along the Memorial Bridge near Memorial Circle in Arlington, Virginia, the proposed site for U.S. President Donald Trump's "Triumphal Arch", seen from the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 8, 2026. REUTERS/Eric Lee/File Photo
President Donald Trump's biggest justification for his towering arch near Arlington National Cemetery is missing from the final blueprints, a new report says.
Final plans posted by the National Capital Planning Commission make no reference to drones, snipers or ammunition storage that Trump promised would turn the 250-foot structure into a "top grade" military complex, The Washington Post reported. The documents, supplied by the Interior Department, instead lay out tourist visits and other ceremonial uses for the monument.
A White House official, granted anonymity to discuss the ongoing project, pushed back on the idea that Trump had changed course. The official said the administration had no plans to release national security details about the arch at this point in the review process.
Interior Department spokesperson Katie Martin told The Post in an email that the arch as designed "is capable of accommodating the national security functions" Trump touted in his Truth Social post. The Pentagon sent questions back to the White House.
Trump announced the military plans on Sept. 20, prompting alarm from aviation safety experts, local officials and advocacy groups. The arch would sit close to Reagan National Airport, and experts have cautioned that drones launched from it would add risk to some of the busiest airspace in the country.
According to The Post, Trump administration officials later told advocates in a meeting that they did not know of any concrete plans to make the arch a military site.
The commission, which Trump has packed with allies, could approve the project at a Nov. 5 hearing. Its synopsis lists a few updates, such as turning the torch held by a Lady Liberty statue atop the arch into an "eternal flame," along with changes to lighting and traffic. But the commission added that "no other plan elements have changed."
Preservationists argue that militarizing the arch would trigger a fresh round of scrutiny. "A new or supplemental review would be required," DC Preservation League Executive Director Rebecca Miller wrote to the Trump administration last month.

Trump's enormous Washington arch gets new blueprints — but where are the drones and snipers? - The Daily Bo Snerdley
sources.text:
THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do).
- Newly released federal planning documents detail Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.
- The publicly released plans omit the drones, sniper positions and other military features Trump previously said would be included.
- The White House disputes claims that the security concept has been abandoned, while federal planners prepare to review the monument in November.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time).
President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is getting closer to becoming one of the most recognizable landmarks in Washington.
But there’s a little mystery in the latest blueprints.
Where did the snipers go?
And what happened to the drones?
The Trump administration released updated plans Friday for the proposed 250-foot monument near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and Arlington National Cemetery.
The project has been promoted as a grand ceremonial gateway celebrating America’s history and national achievements.
Its latest planning documents include renderings, visitor information and details about the monument’s ceremonial features, including a proposed eternal flame.
But something conspicuous is missing.
There is no publicly described military complex.
That is noteworthy because Trump previously announced that the arch would serve a national-security purpose, complete with military personnel and equipment.
In September, Trump declared that he had agreed to convert the monument into a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch.”
He attributed the decision to a request from the military and said the complex would include security features such as drone facilities and positions for snipers.
That raised an obvious question.
Was the administration building a monument, a military installation or some combination of the two?
Friday’s published plans don’t fully answer it.
The Washington Post reviewed the new documents and reported that the military features previously described by Trump are not mentioned.
The Interior Department is overseeing the project, while the National Capital Planning Commission is responsible for reviewing major federal construction proposals in the capital region.
The latest materials emphasize ceremonial use, visitor access and the monument’s architectural significance.
The White House, however, disputes the suggestion that the military features have been abandoned.
An administration official indicated that security considerations remain part of the project, even if they are not detailed in the documents now available to the public.
That explanation is plausible as a security matter: Governments do not ordinarily publish every protective measure associated with sensitive locations.
But it still leaves a distinction between what the president publicly promised and what federal planners have actually disclosed.
The proposed location is significant.
It would sit near Memorial Circle on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, close to Arlington National Cemetery and the bridge leading toward the Lincoln Memorial.
At 250 feet tall, the arch would be a substantial addition to the capital’s monumental landscape.
Its scale has already prompted questions about cost, traffic, architecture, historical preservation and the surrounding views.
Supporters argue that the nation deserves another grand landmark celebrating American history.
Critics question the location, dimensions and the president’s unusually personal role in the design.
And now the architectural debate includes a security question that sounds more like a scene from a Hollywood action movie.
Trump’s September announcement described a monument with capabilities associated with a military installation.
The latest public paperwork describes something much closer to a monumental ceremonial structure.
Those two concepts are not necessarily incompatible, but the federal government has not publicly reconciled all the details.
The National Capital Planning Commission is scheduled to review the proposal November 5.
That process will give planners and the public another opportunity to examine the monument’s design and potential impact.
It will not necessarily reveal sensitive security features, if such features remain part of the proposal.
So, for the moment, the arch has a proposed height, a prominent location, elaborate renderings and an eternal flame.
What it doesn’t have in the publicly released plans is the military equipment Trump previously described.
Perhaps the snipers are still coming.
Perhaps the security concept will be developed separately.
Or perhaps Washington is discovering that designing a national monument becomes a little more complicated when the president also wants it to double as a fortress.
DBS WIRE SOURCES (I’ve got all day).
- Washington Post — New arch plans omit previously described military features
- CBS News — Trump’s original military-complex announcement
- National Capital Planning Commission — Federal monument planning and reviews
